A rare silvery-white metallic element belonging to the lanthanide series of the Periodic Table, which becomes strongly magnetic at low temperatures. Its symbol is Gd, atomic number 64, G atomic weight 157.25, melting point 1313 °C (1586 K), boiling point 3273 °C (3546 K) and specific gravity from 7.8 to 7.896. It occurs with other rare earth elements in many minerals, such as monazite, samarskite, gadolinite and some varieties of Norwegian ytterspar. It is the 41st element in order of abundance in Earth's crust.

The ratio of the output signal strength of a circuit or system to the input or the output voltage of an amplifier compared to its input voltage or the mean ratio of the signal output of a system to the signal input of the same system. It may also be defined on a logarithmic scale, in terms of the decimal logarithm of the same ratio ("dB gain"). Voltage Gain = Output Voltage/Input Voltage. It is a measure of amplification.

A monosaccharide, with the molecular formula C6 H12 O6 , density 1.723 g/cm3 and melting point, 167 °C (440 K). It is a six- carbon sugar that is a constituent of lactose. It occurs naturally as one of the products of other sugars, for example , inlactose , i n polysaccharides and in glycolipids, carbohydrate-containing lipids that occur in the brain and other nervous tissues of most animals.

A refracting telescope having one convex lens and one concave lens. The concave lens serves as the occular lens or the eyepiece with a short focal length; while the convex lens serves as the objective lens with a large focal length. The lenses are situated on either side of a tube such that the focal point of the occular lens is the same as the focal point for the objective lens. Galilean telescopes are shorter than equivalent Keplerian telescopes and give bright, upright images, but they have a limited field of view, spherical and chromatic aberration and, except at low magnification (about 30× or less), poor eye relief. eyepiece objective lens virtual image at infinity f I1 efoFoFe Galilean telescope eye.

A set of equations for transforming the position and motion parameters from a frame of reference with origin at 0 and coordinates ( x , y , z , t ) to a frame with origin at 0' and coordinates at ( x' , y' , z ', t '). They are: x ' = x - vt , y ' = y , z ' = z , t' = t . It is used to transform between the coordinates of two reference frames which differ only by constant relative motion within the constructs of Newtonian physics.

A colourless crystalline aromatic compound, with the chemical formula C6 H2 (OH) 3 COOH, density 1.7 g/cm3 (anhydrous) and melting point 250 °C (523 K). It occurs in gallnuts, sumac, witch hazel, tea leaves, oak bark and other plants and also as part of tannins. It is used to make ink and dyes and on heating yields pyrogallol. It acts as an antioxidant and helps to protect cells against oxidative damage. It is also used to treat albuminuria and diabetes.

A semiconductor alloy of gallium and arsenic, with the chemical formula GaAs and a melting point of 1,238 °C (1,511 K). It has semi-conducting properties similar to or superior to those of silicon, for example, its chips require less electric power and process data faster than those made from silicon. It is used in G lasers, photocells and microwave generators and in high frequency applications such as cellphones, DVD players and fibre optics.

An electromagnetic radiation emitted by excited atomic nucleus when it moves to a lower excitation state. Gamma radiation lies above X-Rays in the electromagnetic spectrum. It is emitted by the hottest part of the universe and also emitted by the radioactive decay of certain materials like cobalt^-60, zinc^-65, caesium^-137, and radium^-226. Cadmium^-109 is also a common source of gamma radiation. Gamma rays can be produced in laboratories by exciting nuclei of a radioactive element by the use of cyclotron and synchrotron. Gamma radiation is one of the three types of radiation resulting from natural radioactivity. It is the most energetic form of electromagnetic radiation, with the shortest wavelength (high frequency). Gamma radiation ranges in energy from about 10 -15 to 10 -10 joule (10 keV to 10 MeV) corresponding to a wavelength range of about 10 -10 to 10 -14 metre. It is so highly penetrating that 25mm of lead only halves its strength. The speed of gamma rays is equal to the speed of light since it is a type of electromagnetic wave and all electromagnetic waves travel with the speed of light. Gamma rays produced in space are absorbed by the earth's atmosphere. Gamma radiation is used for cancer treatment and for diagnostic purposes. They are also used for killing the harmful bacteria in food (a process called food irradiation) so that it can be preserved for longer duration. It is also used for inspection of castings and welds, etc.

An acid found in the central nervous system, predominantly in the brain, where it acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter. Its molecular formula is C4 H9 NO2 , density 1.11 g/ml, molar mass 103.120 g/mol, melting point 203.7 °C (477 K) and boiling point 247.9 °C (521 K). There are two general classes of GABA receptor known as GABA A in which the receptor is part of a ligand-gated ion channel complex; and GABA B metabotropic receptors, which are G protein- coupled receptors that open or close ion channels via intermediaries (G proteins). A third one, GABA C is an ionotropic receptor functions for neuronal inhibition.
A power series with many zero coefficients.

One of three classical states of matter, which has no fixed shape or volume and always fills the whole of the space in which it is contained. It has a density of about 0.1 that of liquids. A gas is distinguished from liquids and solids by the vast separation of the individual gas particles. A substance exists as a solid near absolute zero temperature, but boils into a gas when heated to its boiling point. The average kinetic energy ( KE = nkT ) of a gas is too high for the intermolecular force of attraction to hold the molecules together. That is why molecules of gas are further apart from one another. The shape and size of gas is determined by the containing vessel in which it is introduced.

A technique used for the separation and analysis of complex mixtures of volatile organic and inorganic G compounds. There are two types: gas-solid chromatography in which the stationary phase is a solid; and gas-liquid chromatography in which the stationary phase is a non-volatile liquid. Most compounds with boiling points less than about 250 °C (523 K) can be readily analysed by this technique.

The laws that relate the pressure, volume and temperature of a gas. These relationships have been formulated into what is known as Charles' law, named after J.A.C. Charles (1746-1823). Boyle's law named after Robert Boyle; and Pressure law. They combine to form the General Gas Laws. Charles's law states that, at constant pressure, the volume V of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute (Kelvin) temperature T , or = k ; and Boyle's law states that, at constant temperature, the pressure P of a gas varies inversely with its volume V or PV = k , where k is a constant. The relationship is used to calculate unknown variables rather than by measurement, i.e. = = .

A device for measuring temperature in which the working fluid is a gas such as hydrogen or helium. The gas is enclosed in a glass or fused-quartz bulb connected to a mercury manometer. The pressure exerted by a constant volume of a gas is used for the measurement of temperature of the bath in which the bulb containing the gas is immersed. Temperature t° on this scale is defined as , where P o , P100 and P t are the pressure exerted by the gas when at ice point, steam point and at temperature t respectively.

A synthesis of an aldehyde from an aromatic or heterocyclic compound, hydrogen cyanide, hydrogen chloride and a catalyst of aluminium chloride or zinc chloride. It is a variation of the Sandmeyer reaction for preparing chloro- or bromoarenes by reaction of the diazonium compound. In the Gattermann reaction ,the aromatic amine is added to sodium nitrite and the halogen acid (10 °C), then fresh copper powder (e.g. from Zn+CuSO4 ) is added and the solution warmed. The diazonium salt then forms the haloarene, for example, C6 H5 N2 +Cl- C6 H5 Cl+N2 . The copper acts as a catalyst.

1. A standard or scale of measurement. 2. The width of a railway or tramway track. 3. A standard dimension, quantity or capacity. 4. An instrument for measuring or testing. Also known as valuation , it is a mapping g from an integral domain E \ {0} into the non-negative integers, such that g ( ab ) ≥ g ( a ) for all a and b in E \ {0} and such that for b in E and a in E \ {0} there exist q and r in E for which b = qa + r and either r = 0 or g ( r ) < g ( a ). A law formulated by Carl Friedrich Gauss in 1835 relating the distribution of electric charge to the resulting electric field. It states that the total electric flux normal to a closed surface in an electric field is proportional to the algebraic sum of the electric charges within the surface. A similar law applies to the surfaces, drawn in a magnetic field and the law can be generalised for any vector field through a closed surface. It is one of four of Maxwell's equations which form the basis of classical electrodynamics; the other three being Gauss's law for magnetism, Faraday's law of induction and Ampère's law with Maxwell's correction. Gauss's law can be used to derive Coulomb's law and vice versa.

An integral domain in which every non-zero non-unit is uniquely representable as a finite product of irreducible elements, up to permutation. Since the Gaussian integers are a Gaussian domain and 5 = (1 + 2 i )(1 - 2 i ), 5 is reducible in the Gaussian integers; 3 is irreducible therein and hence prime, because it is in a Euclidean domain.

A two-dimensional method for representing complex numbers by Cartesian coordinates x , y . Along the x -axis or horizontal axis are plotted the real numbers and along the y -axis or the vertical axis the non-real or imaginary numbers. The number x + iy is represented by the point ( x , y ) or by the corresponding vector. If the polar coordinates of ( x , y ) are ( r , θ ), r is the modulus and θ the argument of x + iy .

A system of units for the Gaussian system (electric and magnetic quantities based upon electrostatic and electromagnetic units). In this unit, the electric and magnetic constants are both equal to unity. For example, one Gaussian unit of capacitance (statfarad) =1.112 650~pF; electric potential (statvolt) = 299.792 5~V; and electric charge (statcoulomb) =333.564 1~pC.

The principle or law named after the French chemist, Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac that, when gases combine in a chemical reaction, both reactants and products do so in simple ratios of their volumes and that any gaseous product is also produced in a simple ratio or that when gases react, they do so in volumes which bear simple whole number ratios to one another and to the volume of the product, if temperature and pressure remain constant.

A translucent, yellowish-white hydrous carbonate mineral, with the chemical formula Na 2 Ca(CO3 ) 2 ·5H2 O. It crystallises in the monoclinic system. It is an unstable mineral which dehydrates in dry air and decomposes in water. It is formed as an evaporite from alkali lake waters.

A type of size exclusion chromatography in which molecules in solution are separated based on their size or hydrodynamic volume, using an aqueous solution to transport the sample through the column. Gel filtration is used mainly to separate polar or water soluble polymers and macromolecules such as proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides.

1. Making a theory or hypothesis that what one observes in a special single case applies more widely to form an essential basis of all valid deductive inferences. For example, after studying how one acid reacts with a metal, one draws the conclusion that all acids react with the metal that way. Generalisations postulate the existence of a domain or set of elements, as well as one or more common characteristics shared by those elements. 2. The extension of a number of results to form a rule. For example, the computations 3 + 5 = 5 + 3 and 1.5 + 2.7 = 2.7 + 1.5 could be generalised to a + b = b + a . 3. In logic, universal generalisation is any statement ascribing a property to every member of a class. Existential generalisation is any statement ascribing a property to one or more members of a class. 4. The act or process of perceiving similarity or relation between different stimuli, as between words, colours, sounds, lights, concepts or feelings. 5. Stimulus generalisation is the act or process of responding to a new stimulus by an organism similar to but distinct from the conditioned stimulus. 6. Response generalisation is the act or process of an organism making a different but similar response to the same stimulus. 7. Mediated generalisation is the act or process of responding to a stimulus not physically similar to the conditioned stimulus and not previously encountered in conditioning.

G.definition: The ratio of the maximum likelihood of drawing a given sample under a given hypothesis to the maximum likelihood of drawing that sample under the hypothesis that the given hypothesis is false. The term is also sometimes used for the inverse of this ratio.

If this ratio is always greater than unity, then the series diverges, allowing the limit to be placed in the preceding limit by an appropriate limit inferior or limit superior. When p = 2 and σ = √2α, this becomes Student's t-distribution with 2 degrees of freedom.

In mathematics, a generating function f ( x ) is a formal power series for a sequence, f ( x ) = anxnn = 0 ∞ ∑ , whose coefficients are the given sequence { a 0 , a 1 ,...}. This is often used in the study of the sequence by analytic techniques in both combinatorics and analysis. For example, the generating function for the Fibonacci numbers is x + x 2 1 - ( x + x 2 ) .

1. The members of a family, a group of animals that have similar ages, all the people of about the same age within a society or within a particular family; or a stage or degree in a succession of natural descent such as a grandfather, a father and the father's son comprising three generations. 2. In technology, it is the stages of successive improvement in the development of a technology such as the internal combustion engine or successive iterations of products with planned obsolescence, such as video game consoles or mobile phones. 3. The act of producing offspring, also known as procreation . 4. In physics, it is one stage of a chain reaction involving the splitting of one atom. It takes 10 21 generations in 10 -9 seconds to have an atomic bomb.

1. The interval between the beginnings of consecutive cell divisions, which may be as short as 20 minutes in bacteria or the time interval required for a population to double. 2. The mean time required for a neutron arising from fission to produce a new fission.

In respect to radiation, they are effects, mainly mutations present in the offspring of those exposed to or produced by the absorption of ionising radiation's. Currently, these effects are additive and irreversible.

The effect, predicted by the general theory of relativity in which a mass distorts space- time. The geodetic effect represents the effect of the curvature of spacetime, predicted by general relativity, on a vector carried along with an orbiting body. For example, the vector could be the angular momentum of a gyroscope orbiting the Earth, as carried out by the Gravity Probe B experiment. The geodetic effect was first predicted by Willem de Sitter, Dutch astronomer and mathematician (1872-1934) in 1916, who provided relativistic corrections to the Earth-Moon system's motion. De Sitter's work was extended in 1918 by Jan Schouten, Jan Arnoldus Schouten (1883-1971) Dutch mathematicians and in 1920 by Adriaan Fokker (1887-1972), Dutch physicist.

The distribution of the number of independent Bernoulli trials before a successful result is obtained. In probability theory and statistics, the geometric distribution is either of two discrete probability distributions: the probability distribution of the number X of Bernoulli trials needed to get one success, supported on the set {0, 1, 2, 3, ...}; and the probability distribution of the number Y = X^-1 of failures before the first success, supported on the set {0, 1, 2, 3, ...}.

G.definition: The theorem that in n -dimensional Euclidean geometry, disjoint convex sets lie entirely on opposite sides of some closed hyperplane. This requires one of the sets to have a non-empty topological interior.

The average of a set of n values described mathematically as the n th root of the product of the positive numbers. For example, the geometric mean of two numbers, say 2 and 8, is the square root of their product expressed as 2 × 8 = 4.

A geosynchronous orbit directly above the Earth's equator (0° latitude), from west to east at an altitude of approximately 35,900 kilometres and at a speed matching that of Earth's rotation, thus remaining stationary in relation to Earth. Communication satellites and weather satellites are often given geostationary orbits, so that the satellite antennas that communicate with them do not have to move to track them, but can be pointed permanently at the position in the sky where they stay. Due to the constant 0° latitude and circularity of geostationary orbits, satellites in GEO differ in location by longitude only.

An alcohol, with the chemical formula C9 H15 CH2 OH, density 0.889 g/cm3 , melting point 15 °C (288 K) and boiling point (229 °C, 502 K). It is present in a number of essential oils such as rose oil, palmarosa oil and citronella oil and also in small quantities in geranium and lemon. It is a clear to pale-yellow oil, with a rose-like odour and insoluble in water, but soluble in most common organic solvents. It is used in perfumes; and also in flavours such as peach, raspberry, grapefruit, red apple, plum, lime orange, lemon, watermelon, pineapple and blueberry.

The result that all the eigenvalues of a matrix { a ij } lie within the circles centred at a ii and with radii R i = a ij i = j ∑ . In addition, the union of any k of these circles, if disjoint from the remaining circles, contains exactly k characteristic values counting multiplicity.

Denoted by G , it is a measure of the energy that would be liberated or absorbed during a reversible process or a measure of the capacity of a system to do work, such as the likelihood of a particular chemical reaction to form products. It is expressed as G=H-TS , where H is heat content, T is thermodynamic temperature and S is entropy.

Named after the American theoretical physicist and chemist Josiah Willard Gibbs (1839-1903), it is the necessary behaviour of partial sums of a Fourier series near a jump discontinuity of a function of bounded variation; since convergence is not uniform the curves of the partial sums tend to approximate vertical segments longer than the jump, by a proportion of precisely π sin x x π ∫ dx = 1.17898...

A rule stating that the number of degrees of freedom in a material system at equilibrium is equal to the number of components minus the number of phases plus the constant 2. It is expressed by the equation: F = C - P + 2, where C is the number of chemically distinguishable components present, P is the number of phases in equilibrium and F is the number of degrees of freedom of the system, i.e. the number of independently variable intensive properties that must be specified in order to describe completely the state of the system. For example, the system of water vapour, liquid water and solid ice has zero degrees of freedom because the three phases of vapour, liquid and solid coexist in the one component, water.
An equation describing the relationship between the chemical potentials of species in a mixture named after Josiah Gibbs and Pierre Duhem.

A measurement of inequality in the distribution of incomes for a given population named after its developer, Corrado Gini, an Italian statistician. Its symbol is I G . Graphically, the Gini index is represented by the surface area between a line at 45˚ and the Lorenz curve. The Gini coefficient is zero if there is no inequality in income distribution and a value of 1 if the income distribution is completely unequal, so that 0 ≤ I G ≤1.

A metric system of units devised by A. Giorgi in 1901, because electric measurements could not be explained in terms of the three fundamental units of length, mass and time. Giorgi units are based on the metre, kilogram and the second derived from the earlier centimetre-gram-second (cgs) units. The electrical unit chosen to augment these three basic units was the ampere and the permeability of space (magnetic constant) was taken as 10 -7 Hm^-1 . To simplify electromagnetic calculations the magnetic constant was later changed to 4 π × 10 -7 Hm^-1 to give the rationalised MKSA system. This system, with some modifications, formed the basis of SI units, now used in all scientific work.

White or colourless monoclinic crystals, with the chemical formula Na 2 SO4 ·10H2 O. Upon exposure to fairly dry air it effloresces, forming powdery anhydrous sodium sulfate. It is water soluble, has a salty, bitter taste and is sometimes used in medicine as a mild laxative.It is also used in dyeing.

A consortium of international telecommunications companies formed in 1991 to provide a worldwide satellite-based telephony service. Together with Iridium, ICO and others, Globalstar is one of the new comsat companies supporting global mobile voice and data communications with a constellation of satellites in low Earth orbit. The Globalstar constellation, launched in 1998-99, consists of 48 satellites (with four in-orbit spares) in 1,400-km-high orbits inclined at 52°, allowing a concentration of coverage over the temperate regions of Earth from 70° S to 70° N. The satellites operate in the L-band.

The volume of fluid that is filtered from the capillaries of the glomeruli into the kidney tubules per unit time. It is influenced chiefly by blood pressure and by changes in the diameter of arterioles in the glomeruli. In humans, GFR is about 125ml/min and about 99% of this is reabsorbed as it passes along the kidney tubules to form urine.
A dense cluster or a dense, headlike cluster of sessile or subsessile flowers. Glomerulate means arranged in very small, dense cluster.

An optically active organic compound, with the molecular formula C6 H12 O7 and melting point 131 °C (404 K). It is made by the reaction of certain moulds or a soluble crystalline organic acid, which is an oxidation product of glucose. Gluconic acid occurs widely in nature because such species arise from the oxidation of glucose. It is used in paint strippers.

A colourless, odourless and hygroscopic crystalline compound, with the molecular formula C2 H4 O3 , density 1.27 g/cm3 , melting point 75 °C (348 K) and decomposes at boiling point. It is highly soluble in water. It is a substrate that is oxidised during photorespiration in C3 plants. It is formed by the oxidation of ribulose bisphosphate to phosphoglyceric acid and phosphoglycolic acid. It occurs in sugar cane and sugar beet. It can be made by the electrolytic reduction of oxalic acid or by boiling a solution of sodium monochloroethanoate. It is used in various skin- care products, in making textiles and leather and for cleaning metals.

An ester of glycerol (propane^-1,2,3-triol) in which a hydroxyl group is replaced by a fatty acid. They are subdivided into triglycerides, 1,2- or 1,3-diglycerides and 1- or 2-monoglycerides, according to the number and position of acyl. Glycerides are one of the four main types of complex lipids. Soaps are formed from the reaction of glycerides with sodium hydroxide. H OH C H H OH C H OH C H.

A colourless, sweet and sticky liquid that is soluble in water, which is a basic component of nearly all complex lipids. Its chemical formula is C3 H8 O3 , density 1.261 g/cm3 , melting point 17.8 °C (291.0 K) and boiling point 290 °C (563 K). Gravity is one of the four fundamental interactions of nature. The others are the strong force, electromagnetism and the weak force. Gravity is the agent that gives weight to objects with mass and causes them to fall to the ground when dropped. It also causes dispersed matter to coalesce, thus accounting for the existence of the Earth, the Sun and most of the macroscopic objects in the universe. Gravitation is responsible for keeping the Earth and the other planets in their orbits around the Sun; for keeping the Moon in its orbit around the Earth; for the formation of tides; for natural convection, by which fluid flow occurs under the influence of a density gradient and gravity; for heating the interiors of forming stars and planets to very high temperatures; and for various other phenomena observed on Earth.

A body that emits radiation of all wavelengths at a given temperature, which is a constant fraction of the energy of black-body radiation of the same wavelength at the same temperature. A theorem in mathematical logic that indicates a correspondence between semantic truth and syntactic probability in first-order logic. It is the result that a theory is consistent if and only if it has a model. It was first proved by Kurt Gödel in 1929.

Two theorems of mathematical logic that establish inherent limitations of all but the most trivial axiomatic systems for mathematics. The propositions are undecidable, using only the axioms of that G mathematical structure. The first incompleteness theorem states that no consistent system of axioms whose theorems can be listed by an "effective procedure" essentially, a computer program is capable of proving all facts about the natural numbers. For any such system, there will always be statements about the natural numbers that are true, but that cannot be proved within the system. The second incompleteness theorem shows that if such a system is also capable of proving certain basic facts about the natural numbers, then one particular arithmetic truth the system cannot prove is the consistency of the system itself. The theorems, proven by Kurt Gödel in 1931, are important both in mathematical logic and in the philosophy of mathematics.

This theorem also means that somewhere on the Earth's surface there has to be a point where the horizontal wind speed is zero, even if it's windy everywhere else.

A separate equation showing which substance gains (reduction) or losses (oxidation) an electron at the electrodes of a chemical cell or in electrolysis in a redox reaction. For example, in the equation CuSO4 + Zn → ZnSO4 + Cu, the oxidation half-reaction is given by Zn → Zn 2+ + 2e; the reduction half-equation is given by Cu 2+ + 2e → Cu. The standard way of representing them is the oxidised form + ne - reduced form. A half-equation is balanced by adding or taking away, a number of electrons equal to the total number of charges on the ions in the equation: the number of atoms of each element on the left hand side of the equation must equal the number of atoms of each element on the right hand side of the equation; and the sum of the charges on the left hand side of the equation must equal the sum of the charges on the right hand side of the equation.

A planar region consisting of all points on one side of an infinite straight line and no points on the other side. For example, the line y = mx + c separates the coordinate plane into two half planes; the one above is the graph of y > mx + c and the one below is the graph of y < mx + c . It is the set of points ( x , y ) where ax + by ≥ c or ax + by ≤ c for closed half-planes or corresponding open half-planes or a subset when the line is parallel to an axis, where it is defined as x ≥ a , x ≤ a , y ≥ b and y ≤ b . A closed half-plane is a half-plane that includes the points on the line. If the points on the line are not included, it is called open half-plane .

All points on one side of a hyperplane in a Euclidean or more general space. For example, half Euclidean space is given by the three-dimensional region satisfying x > 0, -∞ < y < ∞, -∞ < z < ∞. If the points on the line are excluded, it is called open half-plane ; if points on the line are included, it is called closed half-plane ; although it may be neither.

The production of a voltage or emf called the Hall voltage within or across a conductor or semiconductor carrying an electric current placed at right angle to a surrounding magnetic field or when there is a strong transverse magnetic field. The voltage is developed because the magnetic field distorts the flow of electrons or other charge carriers that constitute the current, pushing the charged particles to one side of the conductor. Discovered in 1879 by Edwin H. Hall (1855 -1938), it can be used to measure certain properties of current carriers as well as to detect the presence of a current on a magnetic field.

A small rocket engine that uses a powerful magnetic field to accelerate low density plasma and so produce thrust. It is a form of electrostatic propulsion, which in turn is a form of ion propulsion (a category of electric space propulsion). Like gridded ion engines, such as XIPS, Hall thrusters are classified as electrostatic thrusters. Both utilise an inert gas, commonly xenon, as a propellant.

The theorem that a perfect matching exists for a bipartite graph of which all the vertices have the same non-zero degree. It gives a necessary and sufficient condition for finding a matching that covers at least one side of the graph. The theorem also deals with a collection of finite sets, giving a necessary and sufficient condition for selecting a distinct element from each set.

A type of atomic nucleus, in which nucleon (neutrons or protons) are not mixed in the same proportion throughout its volume, but has more of one species than the other. Halo nucleus often contains more neutrons than protons in the stable isotopes of an element. Sometimes, a few of the extra neutrons are only weakly bound to the rest of the nucleus and are relatively far from the centre of the nucleus. Halo nuclei are highly unstable; examples include beryllium^-11 and carbon^-19.

The amount of hydrogen ion present in a water solution is used as a measure of the acidity of a substance; the higher the concentration of hydrogen ion the more acidic the solution and the lower the pH.

A colourless liquid with the chemical formula H2 O2 , density 1.450 g/cm3 at 20 °C, 293 K (pure), melting point^-0.43 °C (273 K) and boils at 150 °C (423 K) with sometimes violent, explosive decomposition. Hydrogen peroxide is prepared commercially by oxidation of alkylhydroanthraquinones and by electrolysis of ammonium bisulfate. It can also be prepared by the reaction of barium peroxide with sulfuric acid and is prepared (with acetone) by oxidation of isopropanol. It is used in dilute aqueous solutions as an oxidising agent, as a mild antiseptic, a bleaching agent and a laboratory reagent. It readily decomposes to give oxygen.

A compound containing the hydrogen tetraoxosulfate(VI) ion with the chemical formula HSO4 - , density 1.84 g/cm3 (liquid), melting point 10 °C (283K) and boiling point 337 °C (610 K). It is an acid salt. It is formed when one hydrogen atom is removed from sulfuric acid (H2 SO4 ) by reaction with a metal, metal salt or organic group. It is used in lead-acid batteries for cars and other vehicles, mineral processing, fertiliser manufacturing, oil refining, wastewater processing and chemical synthesis.

A colourless, poisonous, flammable gas with a sweetish sickly odour similar to rotten eggs. Its chemical formula is H2 S, relative density 1.54 (liquid), melting point^-85.5 °C (187.65 K) and boiling point^-60.7 °C (212.45 K). It is slightly soluble in water and soluble in carbon disulfide. It is produced when organic matter containing sulfur decomposes anaerobically. Hydrogen sulfide is found naturally in volcanic gases and in some mineral waters. It is a part of many unrefined carbonaceous fuels such as natural gas, crude oil and coal. It is obtained as a by-product of refining such fuels. It may be made by reacting hydrogen gas with molten sulfur or with sulfur vapours or by treating a metal sulfide, for example, ferrous sulfide (FeS) with an acid. It is used as an antiseptic, bleach and a reagent. It turns moist litmus paper red and lead ethanoate paper black.

An acidic salt containing the ion HSO3 - with the chemical formula NaHSO3 , density 1.48 g/cm3 and melting point 150°C (423 K). It is used in winemaking to kill yeasts, fungi and bacteria in the grape juice before fermentation to prevent oxidation and to preserve flavour in bottled wine. It is also used as a reducing agent in the chemical industries; in the analysis of methylation status of cytosines in DNA; and also in wastewater treatment to neutralise the residual chlorine before discharging the treated effluent.

A relatively stable inorganic compound of hydrogen and oxygen with the molecular formula H2 O3 present in the atmosphere and possibly also in living tissue. It was first synthesised in 1994 and is produced in a reaction similar to that used for the commercial production of hydrogen peroxide (H2 O2 ) but ozone (O3 ) is used instead of oxygen. Hydrogen trioxide is stable at low temperatures but begins to decompose slowly at^-40 °C forming the high-energy form of oxygen, singlet oxygen.
A type of acid in which the acidic hydrogen is on a hydroxyl group attached to an atom that is not attached to an oxo (=O) group. An example is Si(OH4 ) + H2 O → Si(OH) 3 (O)- + H3 O + .

A colourless solid, with the chemical formula NH2 OH, density 1.21 g cm^-3 (at 20 °C), melting point 33 °C (306 K) and decomposes at 306 K. It is also a functional group where one or more of the hydrogens are replaced by substituents. It explodes on heating and may be employed as an oxidising agent or reducing agent. Hydroxylamine is made by the reduction of nitrates or nitrites and is used in the manufacture of nylon. With aldehydes and ketones it forms oximes.

One of the energy statuses of soil water in which evaporative forces have removed water down to a layer held with 31 bars of tension. It is the maximum amount of hygroscopic water absorbed by 100 g of dry soil under standard conditions of humidity (50 % relative humidity) and temperature (15 °C).

The branch of non-Euclidean geometry that replaces the parallel postulate of Euclidean geometry with the postulate that two distinct lines may be drawn parallel to a given line through a point not on the given line. In hyperbolic geometry, contrary to the parallel postulate, there exists a line m and a point p not on m such that at least two distinct lines parallel to m pass through p . As a result, the sum of the angles of a triangle is less than 180° and, for a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse is greater than the sum of the squares of the other two sides.

Its equation is x 2 a 2 + y 2 b 2 - z 2 c 2 = 1, where a , b and c are constants and the axes of symmetry are taken as the coordinate axes. A phenomenon observed in the elastic and electromagnetic behaviour of materials in which a lag occurs between the application or removal of a force or field and its effect. For example, if the magnetic field applied to a magnetic material is increased and then decreased back to its original value, the magnetic field inside the material does not return to its original value. A hysteresis loop is a closed curve obtained by plotting a graph of the magnetic induction of a ferromagnetic substance (as ordinate) against the external magnetic field. The shape of the curve is characteristic of the magnetic properties of the material and shows the ease with which it is magnetised and the ability to retain magnetisation. The temperature at which pure water freezes or pure ice melts without change in temperature. At this temperature, pure ice and water mixture are in equilibrium at standard atmospheric pressure. It is used as a fixed point (0 °C) on the Celsius scale for defining temperature scales and for calibrating thermometers. To calibrate the ice point of a thermometer, crushed ice is placed inside a funnel that has a beaker or container placed below it to collect dripping water. The thermometer is pushed inside the ice until the top of the mercury thread in the thermometer is just above the ice. When the top of this mercury thread remains stationary for a long period of time, its position is marked on the stem of the thermometer and labelled 0° as the lower fixed point.

A law relating the pressure ( P ), absolute temperature ( T ) and volume ( V ) of an ideal gas. Mathematically, the ideal gas law can be written as: pV = nRT , where n is the number of moles of the gas and R is the gas constant. The ideal gas law implies that at constant temperature ( T ), the product of pressure and volume ( pV ) is constant (Boyle's law) and at a constant pressure, the volume is proportional to the temperature (Charles' law).

1. Inconsistent equations are two or more equations that cannot be solved simultaneously by using one set of values for the variables. For example, the equations x + 2 y = 5 and x + 2 y = 6 as well as 2 x^-3 y = 1 and 4 x^-6 y = 1 are inconsistent as there are no solutions to the systems. If the graphs of equations do not intersect and are parallel, there are no solutions that are true for both equations and are therefore, inconsistent. 2. Of a set of propositions or statements, incapable of all being true at the same time, incompatible. 3. Of a set of well-formed formulae of a formal theory, such that an explicit contradiction may be derived from them by the derivation rules of the theory. 4. Of a formal theory, having an explicit contradiction as a theorem or more generally having an atomic statement as a theorem, whence excluding nothing from its theorems.

Of a function of a single variable, having the property that f ( x ) ≥ f ( y ) for all pairs of arguments such that x > y . If f ( x ) > f ( y ) for all x > y the function is strictly increasing. The symbol is sometimes used to denote either the strict or weak property.

Also known as predictor , in statistics, the variable that defines a set of distinct experimental conditions or that an experimenter deliberately manipulates in order to observe its relationship with some other quantity.

Indeterminate growth is a type of growth characteristic of plants, in which the organism continues to grow as long as it lives. For example, in racemose inflorescence, a plant axis is not limited by development of a terminal flower bud or other reproductive structure and so continues to elongate indefinitely. 2. In mathematics, having no numerical meaning, as 0.00 or 0/0. In an equation, it is defined as having more than one variable and an unlimited number of solutions. 3. In physics, of an effect, not obeying the law of causality. 6. In engineering, of a structure, framework, etc., comprising forces that cannot be fully analysed, especially by vector analysis.

Simultaneous equations which, for some reason, have an infinite number of solutions. Examples are x + y = 4 and 2 x + 2 y = 8, where the two equations are equivalent and x + y = z + 6 y + 3 = 8 z , where there is insufficient data.

A rule for manipulating index numbers when powers are multiplied or divided. Certain index laws must be followed. For example, when multiplying powers of the same term, add indices, for example, a 3 × a 2 = a (3 + 2) = a 5 ; when dividing powers of the same term, subtract indices, for example, a 5 ÷ a 2 = a (5 - 2) = a 3 ; when raising a power of a term to another power, the indices must be multiplied, for example, (a 5 ) 2 = a 10 .

A measure of the magnitude of a variable at one point (in time, for example), to its value at another. In other words, it is a measure of the change relative to some specified base period in some variable such as price, volume, the value of a commodity, the gross national product or the general level of prices. The main application of such numbers are in economics.

Mathematical theories that relate the solutions of an equation to topology associated with the equation. Index theorems are applied to certain problems in the theory of condensed matter, string theory, gauge theories, quantum gravity and super symmetry.
The extended real-valued function defined on a given set that takes value 1 for every element of the set and value 0 for every element not contained in the set. It is denoted i c or δ c .

An equation that determines the index that is used in Frobenius method of solving a second-order ordinary differential equation. It is obtained by noting that, by definition, the lowest order term x k (that corresponding to n = 0) must have a coefficient of zero.

Aerosols may lead to an indirect radiative forcing of the climate system through acting as condensation nuclei or modifying the optical properties and lifetime of clouds. Two indirect effects are distinguished: First indirect effect also known as the Twomey effect is a radiative forcing induced by an increase in anthropogenic aerosols which cause an initial increase in droplet concentration and a decrease in droplet size for fixed liquid water content, leading to an increase of cloud albedo. Second indirect effect, also known as the cloud lifetime effect or Albrecht effect is a radiative forcing induced by an increase in anthropogenic aerosols which cause a decrease in droplet size, reducing the precipitation efficiency, thereby modifying the liquid water content, cloud thickness, and cloud lifetime.

The determination of heights, distances, and other physical objects that cannot be measured directly. There are several methods to do this which include the following: (i) for similar figures, using proportions with a mirror on the ground, or using shadow lengths; (ii) Pythagorean theorem (a 2 + b 2 = c 2 ) method which includes measurement using right-angled triangle; (iii) Thales theorem (if an angle is drawn from the diameter of a circle to the point on its circumference, then, the angle formed is a right angle) by using proportions. Thales derived the following proportion to figure out the height of the Great Pyramid at Giza in Egypt: height of man shadow of man = height of pyramid shadow of pyramid . Indirect measurement can be used to measure so many things such as the width of a river, and the height of tall objects such as trees, pyramids, buildings or mountains.

Its molecules consist of a benzene ring fused to a nitrogen-containing five-membered ring. It occurs in some plants and in coal tar and is produced in faeces by bacterial action. It is used in making perfume and as a reagent.

The electronic effect of the transmission of charge through a chain of atoms in a molecule by electrostatic induction, resulting in polarisation of the bond. Electron donating species such as alkyl groups exert positive inductive effect (+I effect ), while electron withdrawing groups such as carbonyls and nitro groups exert negative inductive effect.

The formula for determining the next term of a sequence from one or more of the preceding terms. For example, the recursive formula for the sequence 5, 20, 80, 320, ... is a n = 4 a n^-1.
A molecular polarisability effect occurring by the inductive mechanism of electron displacement.

A mathematical relationship that makes use of the way in which numbers are ordered or a statement indicating that two quantities are not equal. It is represented by the symbols ≠ (not equal to), ≤ (less than or equal to), ≥ (greater than or equal to), > (greater than), < (less than) ≈ (almost equal to). A conditional inequality is false for some values of a variable while an unconditional inequality is one that is true for all values of the variable. For example, the notation a < b means that a is less than b ; the notation a > b means that a is greater than b and the notation a ≠ b means that a is not equal to b , but does not say that one is greater than the other or even that they can be compared in size.

A characteristic of the post-transition minerals, with the tendency of their outermost s electrons to remain nonionised or unshared in compounds. Examples of post-transition minerals are aluminium, indium, tin, bismuth, lead and thallium.

A measure of an object's resistance to changes to its angular speed or rotation speed. It is the inertia of a rotating body with respect to its rotation. To change the rate of rotation of an object by a certain amount, a relatively large force is required for an object with a large rotational inertia and a relatively small force is required for an object with a small rotational inertia. In automobile engines, flywheels attached to the crankshaft have a large rotational inertia. The engine delivers power in surges; the large rotational inertia of the flywheel absorbs these surges and keeps the engine delivering power smoothly. The moment of inertia plays much the same role in rotational dynamics as mass does in linear dynamics, describing the relationship between angular momentum and angular velocity, torque and angular acceleration and several other quantities. Its symbol is l and its SI unit is kg m^-2 . It is calculated as the sum of the products of the component masses of an object multiplied by the square of their distance from the axis.

1. To make a liquid or gas pass through a substance such as soil by diffusion. Infiltration may be controlled by factors such as cracks, cultivation, freezing, the intensity and type of precipitation and the porosity of the soil. 2. A substance such as fat that gradually accumulates in cells and tissues.

In soils, it is the maximum rate at which rainfall or irrigation water can enter the soil. It is usually measured by the depth (in mm) of the water layer that can enter the soil in one hour. Different soil types have different base rates of infiltration, for example, clay is 10 to 20 mm per hour; for loam to sandy soils, it is 50 mm per hour; for sandy and calcareous (limestone), it is 150 to over 200 mm per hour; and for bare soils, it is 3 to 5 mm per hour. It is lowest when there is no vegetation on the surface. The rate decreases as the soil becomes saturated.

The actual rate at which water is entering the soil at a given time. It may be less than the infiltration rate, because of limited supply of rainfall or irrigation water. It is measured in millimetres per hour (mm/h), just like that of infiltration rate.

The largest member of the set of lower bounds for some given set that is equal to its minimum if the given set has a least member. The infimum of a set T may be defined as satisfying the two conditions, that τ ≤ t for all t in T and that for all t > there is a < t in T. For example, the geometric sequence 1 2 , 1 4 , 1 8 , ... has as a lower bound every real number less than or equal to zero; it has no least member and so no minimum but its infimum is 0.

A negative infinity (-∞) minus any positive number is still negative infinity: -∞- n =-∞ , where n represents any positive number. Subtracting a negative number such as - n from negative infinity (-∞) gives negative infinity (-∞). A part of a geometric figure situated at an infinite distance from the observer, for example, the hypothetical point at which parallel lines meet in Euclidean geometry. 3. This requires bracketing to avoid ambiguity in complex expressions such as '2 + g x 5'. 2. A point on a curve at which the sign of the curvature changes from positive to negative or from negative to positive. In other words, it is a point on a curve at which the curve is oriented concave-upward on one side of the point and concave downward on the order side of the point. If the curve represents the function y = f ( x ), then the second derivative d 2 y dx 2 is equal to zero at the point of inflection.

Its unit is bit, which records no more than the presence or absence of a single feature. 2. An inner automorphism of a group G is a function: f : G G defined for all r in G by an element a in the group or ring by r + a^-1 ra , where a is a given fixed element of G and the operation a^-1 ra is the conjugation. The set of all inner automorphisms of a group form a normal subgroup of the automorphism group that is isomorphic to the factor group of the given group by its centre.

Number of muscle cells per motor neuron. It is variable from muscle to muscle. It is low for fine motor control such as hand muscles and high for gross motor control such as big leg muscles.

A cyclic alcohol that is a constituent of certain cell phosphoglycerides with the chemical formula C6 H12 O6 , density 1.752 g/cm³ and melting point 225 to 227 °C (498- 500 K). The most important isomer is myo-inositol, a water-soluble crystalline compound. It is sometimes classified as a member of the vitamin B complex but can be synthesised by many animals and is regarded as essential nutrients in humans.

A matrix of economic production that shows the relationships between different industries in an economy and to determine whether an economy is productive or non-productive by looking at the Leontief models. In the model, one commences with n goods together with a matrix A whose i , j th entry specifies the number of units of good i necessary to produce one unit of good j . The quantity y = (I - A) x then represents the output of the economy corresponding to input x . This determines whether and how a given net output is feasible by solving the matrix system.

The process by which gas is drawn from the external environment into the lungs through the trachea into the alveoli. In mammals, the rib cage is raised by contraction of the intercostal muscles and the muscles of the diaphragm causing the thorax to enlarge, reducing the pressure in the lung cavity below atmospheric pressure, which causes an influx of air until the pressures are equalised.

The limiting value of the acceleration calculated over a very short time interval at the appropriate instant of time. It can also be defined as the limit of average acceleration as the time interval approaches zero. It is the slope of the tangent of the velocity-time graph at the same instant of time. Instantaneous acceleration is calculated as limΔ v /Δ t 0 = dv / dt = a . Instantaneous velocity is the derivative of displacement or position with respect to time.

A type of field effect transistor ( FET ), which differs from the JFET by the addition of a silicon dioxide layer over the JFET and then a layer of silicon nitride. The result is a device which has even higher input impedance. It has a source, gate and drain terminals like the FET. However, the gate lead does not make a direct connection to the silicon compared with the case for the FET. The gate is a metallic or polysilicon layer atop a silicon dioxide insulator. The gate bears a resemblance to a metal oxide semiconductor (MOS) capacitor. When charged, the plates of the capacitor take on the charge polarity of the respective battery terminals. The lower plate is P-type silicon from which electrons are repelled by the negative (-) battery terminal I toward the oxide and attracted by the positive (+) top plate. This excess of electrons near the oxide creates an inverted (excess of electrons) channel under the oxide. This channel is also accompanied by a depletion region isolating the channel from the bulk silicon substrate. MOSFETS have several advantages over junction transistors as the basic component in integrated circuits. There are fewer steps in processing and there is a smaller area per device. They, therefore, have a greater functional density and lower cost than junction transistors. Other advantages include their high value resistors and their low power dissipation.

A phenomenon exhibited by certain semiconductor devices at low temperatures and high magnetic fields, whereby the Hall resistance becomes precisely equal to ( h / e 2 )/ n , where h is Planck's constant, e is the electronic charge and n is either an integer or a rational fraction. It was discovered in 1879 by American physicist Edwin Hall. The German physicist, Klaus-Olaf von Klitzing discovered the quantum Hall effect, which helps explain electrical movements in atoms, for which he won the 1985 Nobel Prize in physics.

An equation giving the concentration of a reactant or product remaining after a specified time. The rate of reaction is proportional to the rates of change in concentrations of the reactants and products; that is, the rate is proportional to a derivative of a concentration. For each integrated rate law, there is a characteristic plot that can be created which produces a straight line.

The concentration of a reactant or product in a chemical reaction as a function of time (the curve itself). For a zero order reaction: A → products, rate = k, the integrated rate law is [A] = -kt + ln [Ao]. For a first order reaction: A → products, rate = k [A], the integrated rate law is In[A] = -kt + ln[Ao]. For a second order reaction: 2A → products or A + B → products (when [A] = [B]), rate = k[A] 2 , the integrated rate law is 1/[A] = kt + 1/[Ao]. The rate law is the instantaneous rate (the slope of the curve) as a function of concentration. Zero-order reactions are reactions that appear to occur at a rate independent of substrate concentration. First-order reactions are reactions in which the rate varies with concentration of a single species and the change in concentration is exponential, so that a plot of ln(concentration) against time is linear. The stoichiometric coefficient is 1. An example of first-order reaction is radioactive decay, but many electron transfer processes and most enzyme mechanisms contain intermediate reactions that are first order. Second-order reactions are of two types: Second-order reactions of Classes I and II. Second-order reactions of Classes I reactions are reactions in which the rate varies with concentration of a single species, but the stoichiometric coefficient is 2. The rate varies with the reciprocal of the concentration, so that a plot of 1/ (concentration) against time is linear. Second-order reactions of Class II are reactions in which the rate varies with the concentration of two substrates, each of which has a stoichiometric coefficient of 1. A plot of ln(conc.A/conc.B) against time is linear. Examples of second- order reaction are found in many important biological reactions, such as the formation of double-stranded DNA from two complementary strands. Higher-order or Mixed-order reactions are reactions in which more than two species are involved or one species reacts with stoichiometric coefficient >2. Many different classes, of which the simplest involves a single species with stoichiometric coefficient greater than 2. Although many biochemical reactions might appear to be higher-order, in general, the enzyme mechanism functions through binding of multiple substrates to a single protein and the empirical order is simpler and often appears to be zero-order.

Reaction, generally reversible, that involves the penetration of a host material by guest species without causing a major structural modification of the host. Intercalation can refer to the insertion of a guest species into a one-, two- or three-dimensional host structure. The guest species is not distributed randomly but occupies positions predetermined by the structure of the host material. Examples are the insertion of lithium into layered TiS2 [Li x TiS2 (0 ≤ x ≤ 1)] and of potassium into the layers of graphite (C8 K).

The term is also used to refer to the portion of a line lying between two other lines or planes. 2. This intermediate value property, which derivatives also possess by virtue of the mean-value theorem, is also called the Darboux property. It was named after the Czech analyst Bernhard Bolzano (1781-1848).

As a result of the resistance from the source, the output voltage is smaller than the true electromotive force. When a battery fails, it is typically because it has built up enough internal resistance that it can no longer supply a useful amount of power to an external load. The internal resistance of a battery is dependent on the specific battery's size, chemical properties, age, temperature and the discharge current. It has an electronic component due to the resistivity of the battery's component materials and an ionic component due to electrochemical factors such as electrolyte conductivity, ion mobility and electrode surface area. A collaborative venture that effectively divides up the task of collecting, updating and storing the nucleotide sequence data reported by researchers throughout the world. It involves the following computerised databases: DNA Data Bank of Japan (Japan), GenBank (USA) and the EMBL (European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Germany). New and updated data on nucleotide sequences contributed by research teams to each of the three databases are synchronised on a daily basis through continuous interaction between the staffat each of the collaborating organisations.

An equipment calibration standard for making measurements on the Kelvin and Celsius temperature scales, adopted by international agreement in 1968 and revised in 1990, based on thermodynamic temperature and using experimental values to define 16 fixed points. The fixed temperature reference points include the water triple point, the boiling points of oxygen, water, sulfur and the solidification points of silver and gold. ITS^-90 offers defined calibration points ranging from approximately 0.65 K (-272.5 °C), which is the triple point of an equilibrium mixture of orthohydrogen and parahydrogen to approximately 1358 K (1085 °C), which is the freezing point of copper. The ICANN allocates blocks of IP addresses to companies, educational institutions and Internet service providers, which in turn allocate IP addresses to computers that use their Internet connections.

A set of points or real numbers between two specified points or real numbers. A closed interval, [ a , b ], includes the endpoints and so is a set of the form { x : a ≤ x ≤ b }, where a and b are the endpoints, while an open interval, ( a , b ), does not and so of the form { x : a < x < b }. On the real line, the half-open or half-closed interval from a to b is written [ a , b ) or ( a , b ], where square brackets indicate the inclusion of the endpoint (corresponding to a weak inequality the I set notation) and round parentheses its exclusion (corresponding to a strong inequality). Reversed brackets, ] a , b [ are also used for the exclusion. Unbounded intervals are also written in this notation; for example, [ a , ∞) is the unbounded interval x ≥ a is regarded as closed, while ( a , ≥) is the open interval x > a ; the real line, = (∞, -∞), is both open and closed.

1. The difference between the number of births and the number of deaths. It is a measure of the instantaneous rate of change of population size (per individual). Its symbol is r , where r is expressed in numbers per unit time per individual and has the units of 1/time. In a closed population the intrinsic rate of increase is defined as the instantaneous per capita birth rate, b , minus the instantaneous per capita death rate, d . Similarly, in an open population r = (births + immigration) - (deaths + emigration). When per capita births exceed per capita deaths b > d , the population is increasing and r is positive; when deaths exceed births b < d , r is negative and the population is decreasing. 2. The maximum population growth rate.

For example, conjunction introduction is the rule in sentential calculus that permits the inference of the conjunction A & B from the two separate premises A and B; universal introduction is the rule in predicate calculus that permits, under certain conditions, the inference of the universally quantified statement ( x ) Fx from an arbitrary instance Fa .

A value assigned to the size or radius of an ion in a crystal lattice, based on the assumption that the ions are spherical with a definite size. It was developed independently by Victor Goldschmidt and Linus Pauling in the 1920s to summarise the data being generated in X-ray crystallography. Its value is in either picometres (pm) or Angstrom (Å), with 1 Å = 100 pm. Typical values range from 30 pm (0.3 Å) to over 200 pm (2 Å). Pauling's method of calculating ionic radius proved to be the more influential, but in a review of crystallographic data in 1976, a set of ionic radii had been published and these are preferred to Pauling's original values.

A greenish to black powder with the chemical formula FeO, consisting of the element iron in the oxidation state of 2 bonded to oxygen. An odourless, red-brown solid, with the chemical formula is Fe 2 O3 , molar mass 159.69 g/mol, density 5.242 g/cm3 (solid), melting point 1566 °C (1839 K) and decomposes. A physical law expressing the relationship between the heat generated by the current flowing through a conductor, named after James Prescott Joule (1818-89), British physicist. It is the basic principle of some refrigerators. At room temperature, all gases except hydrogen, helium and neon cool upon expansion by the Joule-Thomson process.

A type of field effect transistor (FET) in which the conducting channel lies between pn junctions in the silicon material. A pn junction acts as a diode, that becomes conductive if the gate voltage is reversed. It is the simplest type of field effect transistor (FET). FET is one of the two major categories of transistors; the other is called bipolar junction transistors (BJTs), used as a switch or as a voltage-controlled resistance. The other type of field effect transistor (FET) is called the insulated-gate field- effect transistor ( IGFET ), also known as the metal oxide field effect transistor ( MOSFET ). Insulated gate field-effect transistors are unipolar devices just like JFETs and differs from the JFET by the addition of a silicon dioxide layer over the JFET and then a layer of silicon nitride. The result is a device which has even higher input impedance. The JFET consists of a semi-conductor material flanked by two highly doped layers of opposite type. If a positive voltage is applied to the drain, electrons in the source are attracted into the drain and flow through the channel between the source and drain. As the drain voltage increases, depletion layers associated with the p-n junction increases in size and reduce the cross-sectional area of the channel thus increasing the resistance of the device. When the depletion layers first meet, the drain voltage is called the pinch-offvoltage. At drain voltages above pinch off, the depletion layers extend further into the drain region, but remain essentially constant in the channel. The current therefore remains substantially constant, until the voltage reaches such a value that breakdown occurs. Electrons arriving at the pinch-offpoint, are swept across the depletion layer into the drain region. The resulting drain current characteristics are similar to that of a pentode valve. Applying a negative voltage to the gates will also increase the size depletion layers and hence the pinch J offcondition will be reached at a lower drain voltage and a family of characteristics will be generated for different values of gate bias. The gate voltage is therefore used to modulate the channel conductivity.
